verdict.reasoning: Patient reports symptoms over “the past month or so” and later clarifies “probably a month and a half, maybe two months,” supporting intermittent neurological episodes over 1–2 months.

Patient reports “losing feeling, in my hands and arms… pins and needles” and confirms it is the right hand only; also says “I feel like my arm is getting weaker,” supporting right hand pins and needles/numbness with subjective right arm weakness.

Patient states “at the same time I get my arm symptoms, my leg feels weaker” and notes “my colleague said, I'm walking slightly differently to normal,” supporting weaker legs during episodes and abnormal gait observed by a colleague.

Patient says gait change is “only for three days, or three or four days” and that episodes were “maybe once a week… once a month, but now it's… a couple of times a day,” matching duration 3–4 days and increased frequency to a couple times per day.

Patient reports “I can't hold my cup of coffee. And when I, do drink coffee, it's slightly harder to drink… only during the episodes” and during episodes “I feel like there's something in my throat,” supporting both difficulty with coffee and throat sensation.

When asked about difficulty speaking during episodes, patient replies “No, I can speak fine,” and about visual problems says “I, I don't think so, but I wear glasses,” supporting no dysarthria and no clear visual symptoms.

Patient states “I generally feel tired, and weak. And, sometimes I feel nauseous, and I don't feel like I want to do anything,” supporting intermittent fatigue, generalized weakness, occasional nausea, and low motivation.
When asked if he has symptoms right now, patient says “No, I'm perfectly fine at the moment,” supporting that he is currently asymptomatic.
When asked “do you have any other illnesses at all?” patient answers “No,” supporting no reported past medical history.
Patient says “I take an aspirin, seventy five milligrams, once a day, but that's, because of something I read on the internet,” confirming self-initiated Aspirin 75 mg daily.
In response to allergy query, patient states “I'm allergic to penicillin only,” supporting penicillin allergy.
Patient reports “My, father has had a, operation to the side of his neck, to reduce the risk of stroke,” which is consistent with carotid surgery to reduce stroke risk.

Patient says “I'm, uh, I'm actually a doctor… I work in, uh, plastic surgery,” “No, I live with my wife,” and “No, I don't” to smoking, supporting being a plastic surgery doctor, living with his wife, and being a non-smoker.

Transcript documents recurrent transient right hand/arm pins and needles and weakness, leg weakness with abnormal gait, and difficulty holding/drinking coffee with throat sensation during episodes; doctor’s working diagnosis is “mini-strokes or TIAs, transient ischemic attacks,” supporting recurrent transient focal neurological symptoms with suspected TIA involving right upper extremity, gait change, and transient bulbar-type difficulty.

Patient confirms no current symptoms (“No, I'm perfectly fine at the moment”) and there is a family history of stroke-risk surgery (“father has had a, operation… to reduce the risk of stroke”), supporting no current deficits and family history of cerebrovascular disease.
As noted, patient states he takes “aspirin, seventy five milligrams, once a day… because of something I read on the internet,” indicating self-initiated daily aspirin regimen.

Doctor says “I'm gonna refer you to a, a mini-stroke clinic, or a TIA clinic… they'll usually, call you in within the next one to two days,” supporting urgent referral with expected contact in 1–2 days.

Doctor explains “The hospital, you can actually ring them, on… the PALS number, and then there's also the TIA clinic number. I'm going to leave that number in the notes… And… you can ring them… to find out when they got time to slot you in… to make sure they've got you in the system,” supporting provision of contact numbers and advice to call to confirm scheduling.

Doctor advises “if your symptoms return and they persist, they're prolonged. Then you may need to attend A and E… If… you don't get called… you get in contact back with us,” supporting A&E attendance for prolonged recurrence and contacting GP if delays or issues with the clinic appointment.

Doctor states the clinic will do “an ultrasound of the, carotid arteries… And… they might do a scan of your brain as well… they'll be doing a range of tests in a short time frame,” supporting expedited workup including carotid ultrasound and possible brain imaging to guide further management.
